title: The Secret Life of Electricity
subtitle: Circuits, sparks, lightning and the power in your walls
subject: Physics

p: Right now, electricity is moving inside the walls of your home. It is inside your phone, your fridge, the clock on the wall and even inside you. You cannot see it. You cannot hear it. But flick a switch and a lamp glows. Press a button and music plays.
Electricity is not magic. It is a tiny thing moving. In this book you will find out what that tiny thing is, how we tame it, and how to stay safe around it.
pages.cap: A city at night: every light is electricity at work.
pages.fact: Did you know? Canada uses about 550 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity every year.

p: Everything is made of atoms. Atoms are so small that a single grain of sand holds more atoms than there are people on Earth. Each atom has a centre, and around that centre buzz even smaller bits called electrons.

Electrons carry a tiny electric charge. In some materials, like copper metal, the outer electrons are loose. They can jump from atom to atom. When billions of electrons all drift the same way, that flow is electricity.
pages.cap: An atom: a heavy middle with light electrons around it.
pages.fact: Did you know? An electron is more than 1,800 times lighter than the smallest atom.

pages.h: The loop that makes it go
p: Electricity only flows when it has a complete path, a loop. We call the loop a circuit. A simple circuit has three parts: a battery to push the electrons, a wire for them to travel through, and something that uses the energy, like a bulb.
Cut the loop anywhere and the flow stops at once. That is all a switch does. It opens a gap or closes it. Off means gap. On means loop.
pages.cap: Battery, wire, switch, bulb: a closed loop lights up.
pages.fact: Did you know? The word circuit comes from a Latin word meaning to go around.

pages.h: Flip the switch, and the push arrives almost instantly
p: The electrons themselves crawl along a wire slower than a snail. But the push they pass along races at close to 300,000 kilometres per second. That is why the light comes on the moment you flip the switch.

A battery is a little chemical factory. Inside, two different materials sit in a paste. A slow chemical reaction piles up extra electrons at one end, marked with a minus sign. The other end, marked plus, is short of electrons.
Connect the ends with a wire and the electrons rush from minus to plus. A small AA battery pushes with 1.5 volts. A car battery pushes with 12 volts. Volts measure how hard a battery pushes.
pages.cap: The battery pushes; the switch decides if the push can flow.
pages.fact: Did you know? The first battery was built by Alessandro Volta in 1800 from stacked discs of zinc, copper and salty cloth.

pages.q: What happens when a switch opens a gap in a circuit?
pages.why: Electricity needs a complete loop. A gap breaks the loop, so the flow stops.

p: Some materials let electrons move easily. We call them conductors. Metals are the best. Copper is used in most wires because it conducts well and bends without breaking. Silver is even better, but it costs too much. Aluminum is lighter, so big power lines use it.
Water with salt or dirt in it conducts too. So do you, because your body is mostly salty water. That is why you must keep electricity and water far apart.
pages.cap: Metals carry electricity well; copper wires are everywhere.
pages.fact: Did you know? A single home can hold more than 1 km of copper wire inside its walls.

p: Other materials hold their electrons tightly. Electricity cannot get through. These are insulators. Rubber, plastic, glass, dry wood and dry air are all insulators.

Look at any wire. The shiny copper inside is wrapped in plastic. The plastic keeps the electricity on the road and off your fingers. Workers who fix power lines wear thick rubber gloves tested to 20,000 volts. Birds sit on power lines safely because their bodies do not complete a loop to the ground.
pages.cap: A plastic handle on a hot mug works the same way: it blocks energy from reaching you.
pages.fact: Did you know? Glass insulators the size of dinner plates hold power lines away from their towers.

p: Build a tester and find out what lets electricity through.
steps: Ask an adult for two AA batteries taped end to end (plus to minus), a small 3 volt bulb or LED, and three short wires or strips of kitchen foil.
Tape one wire from the battery minus end to the bulb. Tape a second wire to the plus end. Tape a third wire to the other side of the bulb. Leave the two loose ends apart.
Touch both loose ends to a paper clip. Does the bulb light? Try a coin, a plastic spoon, a pencil tip, a rubber band and a key.
Sort your things into two piles: conductors and insulators.
pages.cap: Your tester is a circuit with a gap. The test object closes the gap.
pages.safe: Do this with an adult. Use only small batteries, and never let the two loose ends touch each other directly: the batteries can get hot. Never test a wall outlet or anything plugged in.

p: Rub a balloon on your hair and stick it to the wall. It stays. You just moved electrons. Rubbing scrapes electrons off your hair and onto the balloon. Now the balloon has extra minus charge and your hair is short of it. Opposite charges pull together, so your hair stands up toward the balloon.
This is static electricity. Static means staying still. The charge sits there until it finds a way to jump.
pages.cap: Opposite charges attract, just as opposite magnet poles do.
pages.fact: Did you know? Static works best on dry winter days, because damp summer air lets the charge leak away.

p: Walk across a carpet in socks and touch a metal doorknob. Zap! A tiny spark jumps to your finger. The shock can measure more than 3,000 volts, which is far more than a wall outlet. So why does it only sting?

Because volts are only the push. The amount of charge is tiny, and it is gone in a millionth of a second. A wall outlet pushes with 120 volts but can keep pushing all day. That is what makes it dangerous.
pages.cap: A doorknob spark is a baby lightning bolt.

p: Inside a storm cloud, ice crystals and hailstones crash together. Just like the balloon and your hair, the crashes move electrons. The bottom of the cloud fills with minus charge. The ground below turns plus. The pull grows until the air itself gives way.
A bolt carries about 300 million volts. It heats the air to around 30,000 degrees Celsius, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. Air that hot explodes outward. That explosion is thunder.
pages.cap: A storm cloud is a battery as big as a mountain.
pages.fact: Did you know? Lightning strikes Earth more than 40 times every second.

p: Light reaches your eyes almost instantly. Sound is slow. It travels about 1 km every 3 seconds. So you can measure how far away lightning is.

See the flash. Count the seconds until the thunder. Divide by three. Ten seconds means the strike was about 3 km away. If you can hear thunder at all, the storm is close enough to strike you. Go inside. Stay inside for 30 minutes after the last rumble.
pages.cap: Thunder takes 3 seconds to travel 1 km.
pages.fact: Did you know? A tree is a poor shelter. Lightning hits tall things first, and wet bark conducts.

pages.q: You see a flash and count 6 seconds before the thunder. About how far away was the lightning?
pages.why: Sound travels about 1 km every 3 seconds. Six seconds divided by three is 2 km.

p: In 1752, Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning is electricity. He then invented a simple way to protect buildings: a pointed metal rod on the roof, joined by a thick wire to a metal spike in the ground.

Lightning hits the rod instead of the roof. The wire gives the charge an easy road into the earth. The building is untouched. More than 270 years later, the CN Tower in Toronto uses the same idea. It is struck about 75 times a year and shrugs every one off.
pages.cap: Tall towers are struck often; metal rods carry the strike safely to the ground.

p: The electric eel of South America is not really an eel. It is a long fish, up to 2.5 m, with thousands of special cells stacked like batteries. Together they can fire a shock of up to 860 volts. That is enough to stun a horse.
Sharks sense the tiny electric signals made by the muscles of hiding fish. Bees pick up the small positive charge of flowers. Even platypuses hunt by feeling electricity with their bills.
pages.cap: Many water animals make or sense electricity in the dark.
pages.fact: Did you know? An electric eel's shock lasts only about two thousandths of a second.

p: Your body is full of tiny electric signals. When you decide to wiggle a toe, your brain sends a pulse down a nerve. The fastest nerve signals travel about 120 m per second. The pulse reaches your toe in a hundredth of a second.

Your heart beats because a small patch of cells sends out an electric tick about 70 times a minute. Doctors can read that tick with a machine called an ECG, and even restart a stopped heart with a carefully timed shock.
pages.cap: A signal jumps from one nerve cell to the next.
pages.fact: Did you know? Your brain runs on about 20 watts of power, enough to light a small LED bulb.

pages.h: Moving electricity makes magnetism. Moving magnets make electricity.
p: Wrap a wire around a nail, connect a battery, and the nail becomes a magnet. Spin a magnet inside a coil of wire, and electricity flows. Nearly all the power in your walls is made the second way.

Behind every outlet is a generator: a huge coil of wire with a magnet spinning inside. Something has to spin it. In Canada, flowing river water does most of the work. About 6 out of every 10 units of Canadian electricity come from water pushing through dams.

Wind turbines spin generators with their blades. Nuclear and gas stations boil water into steam to spin them. Solar panels are different. They turn sunlight straight into electricity with no spinning at all.
pages.cap: Rain fills rivers, rivers push through dams, dams spin generators.
pages.fact: Did you know? Quebec's Robert-Bourassa dam can make enough electricity for about 2 million homes.

p: A power station might be 500 km from your home. To send electricity that far without wasting it, the voltage is pushed up to hundreds of thousands of volts and sent along tall steel towers.

Near your town, a transformer lowers it. Near your street, another one lowers it again, down to the 120 volts that come out of a Canadian wall outlet. All of this happens with almost no moving parts and at nearly the speed of light.
pages.cap: Like a train on tracks, electricity follows a fixed route from station to home.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some Canadian power lines carry 735,000 volts, among the highest in the world.

pages.q: What does the plastic coating on a wire do?
opts: Keeps the electricity inside the wire
pages.why: Plastic is an insulator. It blocks electricity so it stays in the copper and off your hands.

p: Old-style bulbs work by force. Electricity is pushed through a thin coil of metal called a filament. The coil fights the flow and gets so hot, about 2,500 degrees Celsius, that it glows white. Most of the energy leaves as heat, not light.

An LED bulb is smarter. Electrons drop into tiny gaps in a special crystal and give off light directly. An LED that glows as brightly as an old 60 watt bulb uses only about 9 watts, and it lasts 15 times longer.
pages.cap: A glowing filament: light by heat.
pages.fact: Did you know? Thomas Edison tested more than 1,000 materials before finding a filament that lasted.

p: A watt measures how fast something uses energy. An LED bulb sips about 9 watts. A laptop uses about 50. A kettle gulps 1,500 watts while it boils. A whole house, with everything on, might use 5,000 watts or more.

Electricity bills count kilowatt-hours. One kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts running for one hour. That is enough to boil about 10 kettles of water, run an LED bulb for 4 days, or charge a phone roughly 100 times.
pages.cap: A kettle uses more power than 150 LED bulbs.

p: Computers use electricity in a clever way. A tiny switch called a transistor is either on or off. On stands for 1. Off stands for 0. Eight of those switches in a row can spell any number from 0 to 255, or a letter, or one dot of colour on a screen.
A phone chip holds more than 10 billion transistors, each far smaller than a germ. They flip on and off billions of times every second. Every photo, game and message is just patterns of on and off.
pages.cap: Eight on-off switches make one byte.
pages.fact: Did you know? The first transistor, built in 1947, was the size of your thumb.

pages.h: Try it: bend water with a balloon
p: See static electricity pull on something you can watch.
steps: Blow up a balloon and tie it.
Turn on a tap so a thin, smooth stream of water flows.
Rub the balloon on your hair or a wool sweater for 20 seconds.
Slowly bring the balloon close to the stream without touching it. Watch the water bend toward the balloon.
Try it with a plastic comb instead.
pages.cap: The charged balloon pulls on the water molecules, so the stream bends.
pages.safe: Keep the balloon dry and away from your eyes.

p: Electricity is helpful because it is strong. The same strength can hurt you. Remember these rules.

Never poke anything into an outlet. Never touch a switch, plug or device with wet hands, and keep electronics out of the bath. Do not fly kites or climb trees near power lines. If you see a fallen wire, it may still be live even if it looks dead. Stay at least 10 m away, as far as a school bus is long, and tell an adult right away.
pages.cap: Respect the push. Keep water and metal away from outlets.
pages.fact: Did you know? Outlets in Canada now have tiny shutters inside that only open when a proper plug pushes both prongs at once.

pages.q: You find a power line lying on the ground after a storm. What should you do?
opts: Move it off the path with a stick
Stay 10 m back and tell an adult
pages.why: A fallen wire can still carry electricity through the ground around it. Keep far away and get help.

p: More and more things are switching to electricity. In 2024, about one in seven new cars sold in Canada could plug in to charge. A full battery can drive about 400 km, and the car has no engine to rumble.

Electricity is useful because it travels fast, bends around corners through wires and can come from sun, wind and water. Scientists are now building batteries that charge in minutes and wires that lose nothing at all. The tiny moving electron still has surprises left.
pages.cap: Robots, cars, trains and homes all run on the same moving electrons.
pages.fact: Did you know? The fastest electric trains in the world cruise at more than 300 km per hour.

items: electron
A tiny part of an atom that carries electric charge and can move.
circuit
A complete loop that electricity can flow around.
battery
A container of chemicals that pushes electrons out one end and takes them in the other.
volt
A measure of how hard electricity is pushed.
watt
A measure of how fast something uses energy.
conductor
A material that lets electricity flow through it easily, like copper.
insulator
A material that blocks electricity, like rubber or plastic.
static
Electric charge that builds up in one place and stays there until it jumps.
generator
A machine that spins a magnet near a coil of wire to make electricity.
transformer
A device that raises or lowers voltage.

qs: If all the electricity in your town stopped for one day, what would change first? What would you miss most?
Lightning is dangerous, but it also helped people discover electricity. Can something be both a danger and a gift?
Where do you think the electricity in your home should come from in the future, and why?
